These color values range from 0, which means none of that color, to 255, which represents the maximum intensity of that color channel. For example, the RGB value rgb(255, 147, 41) represents an orange color created by combining maximum red, moderate green, and low blue. questions.lessonTitle: Lossy Compression and Original Data Recovery
questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to image compression: lossy compression and lossless compression. Lossy compression, which is used by JPEG, works by throwing away parts of the image data that humans are unlikely to notice. This approach exploits how human vision works, as our eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but tend to blur color together. Because lossy compression permanently removes data, you cannot get the original pixels back once the image has been compressed. However, the tradeoff is often worthwhile because files can become 10 to 20 times smaller with minimal visible difference to the human eye. Lossless compression, used by formats like PNG, preserves every single pixel perfectly while still achieving file size reduction.

questions.lessonContent: PNG (Portable Network Graphics) uses lossless compression to preserve every pixel perfectly while still reducing file size. The PNG compression pipeline combines three distinct tricks that work together sequentially. First, filtering (also called prediction) stores the differences between adjacent pixels rather than their absolute values, taking advantage of the fact that neighboring pixels are usually similar. Second, LZ77 pattern-finding replaces repeated sequences with back-references to previously seen data within a sliding window of the last 32 KB. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, similar to how Morse code uses shorter signals for common letters like E. PNG supports several prediction methods including Sub (predict from left neighbor), Up (predict from above), Average (predict from average of left and above), and Paeth (smartly picks the best option).

The other options describe techniques from other formats like JPEG (DCT, quantization) or are not standard compression methods.

These three steps work together in sequence to achieve significant compression without any loss of image quality.

questions.lessonTitle: The Three Tricks of Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression (used by PNG) preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file. It uses three main techniques to shrink file size: First, filtering or prediction stores how each pixel differs from its neighbor rather than storing absolute values, since adjacent pixels are usually similar. Second, LZ77 finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with back-references, using a sliding window of the last 32 KB to reference previously seen sequences. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, giving common values like 0 (which might appear 60% of the time) shorter codes than rare values. These three tricks form the complete lossless pipeline used by PNG and ZIP files.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG divides an image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components using a mathematical process. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies capture fine details like sharp edges and textures. Since photographs contain mostly smooth gradients, most of the visual information resides in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG exploits this characteristic by keeping the low-frequency data while discarding high-frequency details that humans are less likely to notice. This block-based processing is what creates the characteristic "blocking artifacts" visible when JPEG compression is cranked up to very high levels.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG is a lossy compression format that excels at compressing photographs and complex images. However, it has a significant limitation compared to lossless formats like PNG. While PNG supports a fourth channel called alpha, which controls pixel transparency, JPEG does not include alpha channel support. This means JPEG cannot preserve transparency information in images, making it unsuitable for graphics, logos, or any images that need to be composited over other backgrounds. When transparency is required, PNG or other formats that support alpha channels must be used instead.

To take advantage of this, JPEG first converts pixels from the RGB color format to a different representation that separates brightness from color. Once separated, JPEG can reduce the color resolution since the human eye won't notice subtle color shifts in detailed areas. The brightness information is preserved at full resolution while color information is downsampled, allowing for significant file size reduction without noticeable quality loss in most photographs.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression begins by converting pixel data from RGB format to a different color space that separates brightness from color information. This transformation exploits a key property of human vision: our eyes resolve brightness (luminance) in fine detail but tend to blur color (chrominance) together. Because we notice sharp edges in brightness but are less sensitive to slight color variations, JPEG can reduce color resolution without most people noticing the difference. The algorithm then applies a discrete cosine transform to convert each block into frequency components representing different levels of detail. Low-frequency components capture smooth gradients and overall color tones, while high-frequency components represent sharp edges and fine textures. By treating each 8×8 block independently, JPEG can target specific areas for compression while preserving others. This block-based approach is why heavily compressed JPEG images show characteristic square artifacts.
